lead: Perpendicular vectors behave like clean coordinate axes: each direction is independent of the others. An orthonormal set is a collection of mutual right angles with unit length, so it acts as a ready-made coordinate system. The orthogonal complement of a subspace gathers every vector at right angles to it. These ideas power least squares, QR and SVD.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for inner product and norm, 5.2 for the inequalities, and Unit 2 for basis, dimension, null space and direct sums.

blocks.text: Fix an inner product ⟨u,v⟩ on a real vector space V; the norm is ‖u‖ = √⟨u,u⟩. A set {u1,…,uk} is orthogonal when ⟨ui,uj⟩ = 0 for every i ≠ j. It is orthonormal when also ⟨ui,ui⟩ = 1 for each i.

An orthogonal set of nonzero vectors cannot be dependent. Suppose c<sub>1</sub>u<sub>1</sub> + … + c<sub>k</sub>u<sub>k</sub> = 0. Take the inner product of both sides with u<sub>j</sub>: every term dies except c<sub>j</sub>⟨u<sub>j</sub>,u<sub>j</sub>⟩, so c<sub>j</sub>‖u<sub>j</sub>‖² = 0. Since u<sub>j</sub> ≠ 0, c<sub>j</sub> = 0. All coefficients are zero, so the set is independent.

Independent and spanning its own span, the set is a basis of span{u<sub>1</sub>,…,u<sub>k</sub>}. This is why perpendicular axes are so useful: no vector is wasted, and dimension equals the number of vectors.

Let {e<sub>1</sub>,…,e<sub>n</sub>} be an orthonormal basis of V. Every u in V has one expansion u = Σ c<sub>i</sub>e<sub>i</sub>. Take the inner product with e<sub>j</sub>: only i = j survives, giving c<sub>j</sub> = ⟨u,e<sub>j</sub>⟩. So u = Σ ⟨u,e<sub>i</sub>⟩e<sub>i</sub>.

A square matrix Q is orthogonal when QᵀQ = I, equivalently its columns form an orthonormal set. Orthogonal matrices preserve inner products: ⟨Qx,Qy⟩ = xᵀQᵀQy = xᵀy. Hence lengths and angles do not change, which is why rotations are orthogonal.

For any orthonormal set e<sub>1</sub>,…,e<sub>m</sub> (not necessarily a full basis) and any u, Bessel's inequality holds: Σ<sub>i=1</sub><sup>m</sup> |⟨u,e<sub>i</sub>⟩|² ≤ ‖u‖². When the set is a full orthonormal basis the inequality becomes equality, Parseval's identity: Σ |⟨u,e<sub>i</sub>⟩|² = ‖u‖². The sum is the squared norm of the orthogonal projection of u onto span{e<sub>1</sub>,…,e<sub>m</sub>}.
For a subspace W of V, the orthogonal complement is W⊥ = {v in V : ⟨v,w⟩ = 0 for all w in W}. It is itself a subspace: if v1, v2 are perpendicular to every w, so is αv1 + βv2.
Only the zero vector lies in both. If x is in W and in W⊥, then ⟨x,x⟩ = 0, so x = 0. Thus W ∩ W⊥ = {0}, not the empty set.

Dimensions add: dim W + dim W⊥ = dim V = n. The proof picks a basis of W, extends it to a basis of V (Unit 2), and applies Gram–Schmidt to the whole extended basis, starting with the basis of W; the added vectors then become a basis of W⊥. Since the two subspaces meet only at 0, every v in V splits uniquely as v = w + z with w in W and z in W⊥. We write V = W ⊕ W⊥.

For an m × n real matrix A, the null space N(A) is the orthogonal complement of the row space. A vector x satisfies Ax = 0 exactly when x is orthogonal to every row of A. So row space and null space are perpendicular and their dimensions add to n, which is the rank–nullity theorem again.

figure.caption: The subspace W and its orthogonal complement W⊥ share only 0; a vector in W is perpendicular to both n₁ and n₂.

spec.aria: A two-circle Venn diagram where the subspace W and its orthogonal complement share only the zero vector.

examples.question: In ℝ³ let W = span{(1, 1, 0)}. Find W⊥ and check dim W + dim W⊥ = 3. Also verify that e₁ = (1, 1, 0)/√2, e₂ = (1, −1, 0)/√2, e₃ = (0, 0, 1) is orthonormal, and expand (2, 0, 3) in this basis.
steps: W = {t(1, 1, 0) : t in ℝ}. A vector x = (x, y, z) lies in W⊥ exactly when ⟨x, (1, 1, 0)⟩ = x + y = 0, so y = −x. Thus W⊥ = {(x, −x, z)} = span{(1, −1, 0), (0, 0, 1)}.
dim W = 1 and dim W⊥ = 2, so dim W + dim W⊥ = 1 + 2 = 3 = dim ℝ³. The only common vector is 0.
Check the three vectors: ‖e₁‖ = √(1² + 1²)/√2 = 1, ‖e₂‖ = √(1² + (−1)²)/√2 = 1, ‖e₃‖ = 1. Their pairwise dot products are 0, so the set is orthonormal.
examples.check:
import math
c1=2/math.sqrt(2)
c2=2/math.sqrt(2)
c3=3
print(round(c1,3))
print(round(c2,3))
print(round(c3,3))

traps: An orthogonal set containing the zero vector is not independent; the independence theorem needs the word nonzero.
W ∩ W⊥ is {0}, not the empty set. The zero vector lies in every subspace.
Orthogonal means pairwise dot product zero; orthonormal also requires each vector to have length 1. A perpendicular basis of length-5 vectors is orthogonal but not orthonormal.
Bessel is an inequality for any orthonormal set. Equality for a particular u holds exactly when u lies in span{e₁,…,e_m}; for a full orthonormal basis, Parseval's identity gives equality for every u.
For a matrix, the null space is the orthogonal complement of the row space, not of the column space.
Examiners often ask for dim W⊥. It is n − dim W, not n − 1.

quiz.q: Define an orthogonal set and an orthonormal set in an inner product space.
quiz.a: A set {u₁,…,u_k} is orthogonal if ⟨u_i,u_j⟩ = 0 for all i ≠ j. It is orthonormal if also ⟨u_i,u_i⟩ = 1 for every i.

quiz.q: Define an orthogonal matrix and state one property it preserves.
quiz.a: A square matrix Q is orthogonal if QᵀQ = I. It preserves inner products, hence lengths and angles.

quiz.q: Why is an orthogonal set of nonzero vectors linearly independent?
quiz.a: If Σc_i u_i = 0, taking the inner product with u_j gives c_j⟨u_j,u_j⟩ = 0. Since u_j ≠ 0, c_j = 0 for every j, so the set is independent.

quiz.q: In ℝ³ let W = span{(1, 0, 1)}. Find W⊥ and verify dim W + dim W⊥ = 3.
quiz.a: x = (x, y, z) is in W⊥ when x + z = 0, so W⊥ = span{(0, 1, 0), (1, 0, −1)}. dim W = 1, dim W⊥ = 2, and 1 + 2 = 3.

quiz.q: Let {e₁, e₂, e₃} be an orthonormal basis and u = 2e₁ − e₂ + 4e₃. Use Parseval's identity to compute ‖u‖.
quiz.a: The coefficients are 2, −1, 4. The sum of squares is 4 + 1 + 16 = 21, so ‖u‖² = 21 and ‖u‖ = √21.

quiz.q: Prove that W ∩ W⊥ = {0} for any subspace W.
quiz.a: If x is in both W and W⊥, then x is perpendicular to every vector of W, including itself. So ⟨x,x⟩ = 0, which forces x = 0.

quiz.q: If Q is an orthogonal matrix, show that ‖Qx‖ = ‖x‖ for every vector x.
quiz.a: ‖Qx‖² = (Qx)ᵀ(Qx) = xᵀQᵀQx = xᵀx = ‖x‖². Taking square roots gives ‖Qx‖ = ‖x‖.

beyond: Not for the exam. Orthogonal complements and orthonormal bases are the language of signal processing, computer graphics and numerical linear algebra. In machine learning, projections onto orthogonal complements explain residuals in regression. Search next for orthogonal complement, Bessel inequality, Parseval identity, QR decomposition and pseudoinverse.
